12608-get-next:
Hugh McHugh's 1905 comic sketches, Get Next, illustrated by Gordon H. Grant, follow John Henry through American fads. Contents promise John Henry on race tipsters, bridge whist, amateur photography, the grip, courting, summer resorts and great men. The opening sketch finds John Henry beating the ballast up Broadway, as Pete the Piker chatters about cinches at the track.

Get the saw, Pete, John Henry says, since ponies stung him so hard his bank account looked like a porous plaster. McHugh writes in slangy, first-person humour, each sketch a monologue on a modern craze. The book is light American comedy, best enjoyed as a series of bar-room and streetcar talks.
35067-the-pocket-bible-or-christian-the-:
The Pocket Bible, or Christian the Printer, is a tale of the sixteenth century by Eugene Sue. The Labor News Company published it at New York in 1910. Daniel De Leon translated it from the French. The tale forms one volume of Sue's full series, The Mysteries of the People, a history of a proletarian family across the ages.

The series list runs from The Gold Sickle and The Brass Bell through The Iron Collar and The Silver Cross to The Executioner's Knife and Joan of Arc. The Pocket Bible stands late in the sequence, in two volumes, before The Blacksmith's Hammer and The Sword of Honor. Sue carries his family's story into the age of print and religious war. Christian the printer, with his pocket Bible, works amid the struggles of the Reformation century.
4033-who-spoke-next:
A story told by objects in an old garret turns to a musket with an old republican pride, a weapon that speaks in one short, decided word. Boys Frank and Harry call on their mother for its history, and she reports the musket's scorn for palaver.

The musket recalls service beside the Boston Cadets, the governor's body guard, when crowds of women and children pressed so close that the governor could hardly move. Flourished round bravely by its master, it did bloody work yet felt defiled as never before. The tale charms young readers with a talking relic of American history.
43671-a-history-of-epidemics-in-britain-:
A History of Epidemics in Britain, volume II, continues Charles Creighton's systematic history. The Cambridge University Press published it in 1894. Creighton had been demonstrator of anatomy at Cambridge. The first volume ran from 664 to the extinction of plague. This volume carries the story from 1666 to the present time. Its preface confesses fresh difficulties.

Plague, the earlier theme, was uniform and dramatic. After it, a numerous brood of fevers replaced it. Synochus, nervous, putrid, and miliary fevers crowd the records. Old writers described them dryly, in almost obsolete terms. Creighton's chapter on continued fevers therefore does double work. It distinguishes the fevers' kinds, and it reads society through them. Typhus and relapsing fever, he shows, index working-class conditions exactly. Unwholesome towns, gaols, the navy, dearth, and war prices all register in the fever returns. A special chapter gives Ireland the same close treatment.
60745-the-autumn-after-next:
The Autumn After Next, a fantasy tale by Margaret St Clair, ran in Worlds of If in January 1960. The blurb says that being a wizard missionary to the Free'l needed more than magic; it called for a miracle. Neeshan watches a Free'l spell go wrong: the rite should have drawn the moon down, made water run uphill, and turned the seasons.

The tribe used broor's blood in place of newt's, alganon in place of vervet juice, and missed the solstice by three days, so nothing happened. They stamp in their circle from moonset toward dawn, sure the charm just takes time. Neeshan, who has tried hard to teach them care, steps in with bitter patience. Clair plays the clash of true craft and cheerful sloth for dry wit.
61375-the-historical-geography-of-europe:
The Historical Geography of Europe, Volume One, is the text volume of a two volume work by Edward Freeman, honorary fellow of Trinity College, Oxford. It was printed at London by Longmans, Green and Company in 1881. Freeman is plain in his preface about the book's slow making. It was begun several years before, delayed by loss of strength, absence from England and other work. The early part was even printed some years back.

That delay changed the plan, he owns. He could not treat Europe as a whole throughout, as the first chapters do. His object, he says, is a humble one. The book aims at little more than tracing out the extent of various states at different times. It sets the changes in their due relation to one another and to their causes.
76384-charity-s-birthday-text:
Charity Birthday Text, by Agnes Giberne, was printed in London by the Religious Tract Society. Giberne had written Willie and Lucy at the Sea Side and Hungering and Thirsting. The tale turns on a birthday gift with a verse on it.

It was little Charity Mitchel tenth birthday. Poor Charity had no mother, for Mrs Mitchel had died many years before. Ever since then Charity had lived in London with her father and her only brother. Edwin, a timid, delicate little fellow, was two years and a half younger than herself. He was very fond of Charity, who was a warm hearted, unselfish sister. Charity birthday was quite an event in the quiet household. One was an illuminated card with her text, suffereth long, and is kind. Church readers get a gentle child tale.
8995-what-katy-did-next:
Susan Coolidge wrote this children's novel as a sequel to her Katy Carr tales, for girls who had begged to hear more of Katy after school. Katy, now grown, leaves home to travel with friends, first by sea and then through England, France, Switzerland, and Italy. The trip is both a holiday and a test of her good sense.

Along the way she meets kind strangers, sees famous sights, and learns to bear small trials with grace, from illness to lost plans. Coolidge writes in a warm, easy voice, and the book charms still as a gentle tale of youth, friendship, and growing up on the road.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sext:
Sext, the sixth hour of the Roman day, matches our noon closely. Among Jews it already ranked with Terce and None as an hour most favorable to prayer, and Acts tells how Peter went up to pray at that hour. It was midday, the usual hour of rest, and so a natural pause for prayer. This entry gathers the Fathers' symbolism of the hour, summarized from Cardinal Bona's work on psalmody.

Noon is the hour of the sun at its full, an image of divine splendor and grace. At the sixth hour Abraham received the three angels, image of the Trinity, and Adam and Eve ate the fatal apple. Ambrose urged prayer at noon because divine light then stands at its fullest. Above all, it was the hour Christ was nailed to the cross, a memory that left a visible mark on most of the liturgy for this hour.
doe-osti-3025100-final-project-report-sb:
Robert H Wills of Intergrid, LLC, of Temple, New Hampshire, filed this SBIR Phase II final report in March 2026 for next-generation power converters for distributed wind. The funded period ran from September 2022 through December 2023 on a budget of 1,150,000 dollars, fully spent. Small wind turbines need converters that play well both with the grid and with islanded home systems, and that dual duty drove the designs.

The report's test setting is a working microgrid site: a turbine, three SMA 7.7 kilowatt inverters on the solar array, high-efficiency heat pumps in the house and barn, two electric vehicles, and an electric snow blower. Microgrid switchgear, including the interface device and battery storage, was being installed as the report closed. Collaboration with the Alaska Center for Energy and Power at Fairbanks is also recorded.
get-next:
George V. Hobart, writing as Hugh McHugh, made John Henry the slang-talking hero of a string of comic books. Get Next!, from 1905, gathers sketches with titles like John Henry on Race Tipsters, on Bridge Whist, on Courting, and on Great Men. Gordon H. Grant drew the pictures. Hobart lists a shelf of John Henry books on the title page, from John Henry to You Can Search Me.

In the first sketch, Pete the Piker tries to sell John Henry a sure thing at the track. John Henry, stung once too often, sends the tips to the discards. The talk is fast Broadway slang of 1905, full of bets, jokes, and street wisdom. The humor dates, and that is its charm: a live sample of American comic speech at the start of a new century.
papyrus-of-ani-1913-text:
The Papyrus of Ani, in its 1913 text edition, presents Egypt's most famous Book of the Dead. Ani was a royal scribe in ancient Thebes. His painted scroll guided his soul through the afterlife.

Translator Wallis Budge renders the spells, hymns, and judgment scenes. The dead man's heart is weighed against a feather of truth. Gods, demons, and gates crowd the path to paradise. Budge's versions shaped how the West first read these texts. The scroll remains a funerary treasure, and this edition keeps a classic translation in reach. Its painted scenes remain icons of Egyptian faith.
what-katy-did-next: Here the reader finds a frontispiece note, a dedication, and a contents list, but no chapter text. Susan Coolidge wrote What Katy Did Next for the many girls who begged for more of Katy Carr. Twelve years of pleas, her dedication says, brought the book about. The contents start with a surprise guest and an invitation. Katy then sails on a ship called the Spartacus. Later chapters tour England, cross the Channel, and reach Rome for a holiday.
who-spoke-next:
Mrs. Follen wrote Who Spoke Next, a set of tales in which household things tell their own stories. Frank and Harry call on their mother for the tale of the old musket, as promised. The musket, she says, was proud and slow to speak. It had made itself heard in the world by one short, sharp word.

Deeds, not words, the musket declares, is the motto for all. It recalls no clear sense of life before human craft shaped its parts. Each part, it insists, was perfect of its kind. Follen lets an old gun tell of war and years in a garret. Young readers learn matter and memory from a talking thing.
